notes:
Task and constraints: Apply multiple source-to-target replacements at original indices, skipping replacements whose source does not match.
Idea: Precompute a replacement at each valid starting index, then scan the original string once to build the output.
Technique and why it applies: bucket records the source length and target characters for each start. When a replacement is present, the scan emits its target and skips the consumed source span; otherwise it copies one original character.
Invariant: i is the next unconsumed original position, and bucket[i] describes a valid replacement beginning there.
Edge cases: The source check short-circuits when an index would exceed S. If two operations share an index, the later one overwrites the earlier bucket entry; the usual constraints avoid conflicting indices.
Complexity: Validation costs O(total source characters), and the final scan is O(n+total output); bucket and output use O(n+output) space.

Task and constraints: For every node in a tree, compute the sum of distances to all other nodes.
Idea: Root the tree, use postorder DFS to compute subtree sizes and root distances, then preorder DFS to reroot the distance sums.
Technique and why it applies: A child subtree contributes its own distance sum plus its node count to the parent. Moving the root across an edge increases distances to outside nodes and decreases distances to inside-subtree nodes.
Invariant: tree_nodes[v] is the subtree size, and distances[v] is the distance sum for v after rerooting.
Edge cases: The graph must be a connected tree and n must be positive. Recursive DFS can exceed Python's recursion limit on a long chain.
Complexity: Both traversals visit each node and edge once, giving O(n) time and O(n) adjacency/recursion space.

Task and constraints: Return the sum of distances from each tree node to every other node.
Idea: Run two DFS passes: one computes subtree sizes and root distance totals; the second propagates totals to children.
Technique and why it applies: For child nei, result[nei] = result[node] - count[nei] + (N-count[nei]); moving the root one edge closer to its subtree and farther from all other nodes updates the sum.
Invariant: count[node] is the size of its subtree, and result[node] is the sum of distances from node to all nodes after the second pass.
Edge cases: The input is assumed to be a connected tree with at least one node. Deep trees can trigger recursion-depth limits.
Complexity: O(N) time for two traversals and O(N) space for adjacency lists, arrays, and recursion.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of overlapping 1-cells after translating one binary image over another.
Idea: Record coordinates of all 1-cells in both images and count every relative offset between a cell in each list.
Technique and why it applies: For each pair of ones, their coordinate difference is the translation that aligns them. The most frequent offset maximizes overlap.
Invariant: shiftDict[(dx,dy)] counts pairs of ones aligned by that translation.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used but not imported in the snippet. If either image has no ones, shiftDict stays empty and the function returns zero.
Complexity: With a ones in img1 and b in img2, time is O(n²+ab) and space is O(ab) distinct offsets in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum overlap between two binary square images under translation.
Idea: For each pair of 1-cells, increment a counter indexed by their relative row and column shift.
Technique and why it applies: Each translation aligns a specific set of ones, and the counter measures the number of aligned pairs. The maximum counter is the greatest possible overlap.
Invariant: count[shift] stores the overlap score accumulated for that translation.
Edge cases: The method assumes square images of equal size and nonempty input, because it uses len(A) for both dimensions and calls max(count). If there are no ones, the zero-initialized count array makes the result zero.
Complexity: Comparing all cell pairs takes O(n^4) time and the shift array uses O(n²) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two axis-aligned rectangles have positive-area overlap.
Idea: Reject the pair if one rectangle lies entirely above, below, left, or right of the other.
Technique and why it applies: Positive-area intersection requires strict overlap on both coordinate axes; touching edges do not count as overlap.
Invariant: The condition checks whether any separating horizontal or vertical boundary exists.
Edge cases: Rectangles that only touch at an edge or corner return False. Inputs are represented as [x1,y1,x2,y2].
Complexity: A fixed number of comparisons gives O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether two axis-aligned rectangles intersect with positive area.
Idea: Test interval intersection separately on the x and y axes.
Technique and why it applies: Each axis intersects only when max(left endpoints) is strictly less than min(right endpoints). Both axes must overlap for the rectangles to overlap in area.
Invariant: intersect returns whether the two one-dimensional intervals have positive-length intersection.
Edge cases: Edge-only and corner-only contact return False because the comparison is strict. The method assumes each rectangle has valid ordered coordinates.
Complexity: Constant-time comparisons use O(1) time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the probability of finishing the New 21 Game with a score no greater than n, stopping when the score reaches k.
Idea: Use a sliding window of probabilities for terminal scores from k through k+maxPts-1, then fill probabilities backward.
Technique and why it applies: Each draw adds a uniformly random integer from 1 to maxPts, so dp[i] is the average of the next maxPts probabilities. The deque sum maintains that moving window.
Invariant: s is the sum of the probabilities currently in dp for the next maxPts scores.
Edge cases: collections.deque is used without importing collections in the snippet. The code assumes k and maxPts satisfy the problem constraints.
Complexity: Each state is computed once with constant amortized work, giving O(k+maxPts) time and O(maxPts) deque space.

Task and constraints: Simulate dominoes falling left or right under simultaneous force propagation.
Idea: Use breadth-first layers to propagate L and R pushes to neighboring upright dominoes.
Technique and why it applies: Each wave updates an integer force: left pushes subtract one and right pushes add one. Opposing waves can cancel to zero, leaving a domino upright; nonzero signs determine the final direction.
Invariant: arr[i] accumulates the net directional influence received by position i, and d tracks positions already assigned a push.
Edge cases: If equal-time opposing forces reach a domino, the accumulated value becomes zero. The code relies on layer-wise processing to combine forces that arrive simultaneously.
Complexity: Each position is marked and queued at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the final state of dominoes after pushes spread along the line.
Idea: Sweep left-to-right to accumulate rightward force, then right-to-left to accumulate leftward force.
Technique and why it applies: Force weakens by one per upright cell, resets at an opposing push, and is combined by subtraction. The sign determines whether a domino falls right, left, or stays upright.
Invariant: After both sweeps, force[i] is the net directional force on position i.
Edge cases: Equal opposing forces cancel to zero. Existing L and R dominoes reset force in the opposite sweep so they block the other direction.
Complexity: Two linear passes take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count connected groups of strings that are similar, where similarity means they differ in at most two positions.
Idea: Treat strings as vertices in an implicit graph and use DFS to count connected components.
Technique and why it applies: isSimilar tests whether two strings are adjacent. DFS visits every string reachable through similarity edges; each unvisited start begins a new group.
Invariant: visited contains all string indices assigned to already explored components.
Edge cases: The similarity test accepts any pair differing at most two positions, relying on the problem's anagram constraint for the usual definition. Recursive DFS can exceed recursion depth for large groups.
Complexity: Pairwise similarity checks cost O(n²L) for n strings of length L, with O(n) visited space.

Task and constraints: Count 3-by-3 magic squares inside a grid, where each row, column, and diagonal has equal sum and values are 1 through 9.
Idea: Check each 3-by-3 window for row/column/diagonal sums, distinct entries, and minimum value one.
Technique and why it applies: For a normal 3-by-3 magic square, the target sum is 15 and the entries must be the nine distinct integers 1 through 9. The helper generalizes the expected sum formula using k=3.
Invariant: nums contains values in the current window, while sum_diag, sum_anti, sum_r, and sum_c accumulate its line totals.
Edge cases: Checking only min_num==1 and nine distinct values does not ensure max_num==9 or all values are within 1..9; distinct values plus line sums may constrain this, but the code does not directly enforce the full range.
Complexity: Each 3-by-3 window takes O(1) time, so total O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether all rooms can be visited starting from room zero using keys found inside rooms.
Idea: Use breadth-first search, adding keys from each newly visited room to a queue.
Technique and why it applies: A key to room j creates a directed reachability edge. BFS explores every room reachable from room zero and compares the visited count with the total.
Invariant: visited_rooms contains exactly the rooms processed so far; queue holds discovered keys.
Edge cases: collections is used without an import in the snippet. Duplicate keys may enqueue the same room multiple times, but visited_rooms prevents processing it repeatedly.
Complexity: Each reachable room and key is processed a bounded number of times, giving O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether every room is reachable from room zero using the keys in visited rooms.
Idea: Traverse the room graph with an explicit stack and mark each newly discovered room.
Technique and why it applies: Each key points to a room that can be entered; stack traversal explores all reachable rooms. The visited set prevents cycles and repeated work.
Invariant: lookup contains all discovered rooms, and stack contains discovered rooms awaiting exploration.
Edge cases: A single room returns True because lookup initially contains room zero. The early return occurs when all rooms have been discovered, which is sufficient even before their keys are processed.
Complexity: Each room and key is processed once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) visited/stack space.

Task and constraints: Split a digit string into a Fibonacci-like sequence of at least three nonnegative integers, each no greater than the allowed maximum.
Idea: Enumerate candidate first and second numbers, then recursively consume the exact decimal representation of each next sum.
Technique and why it applies: The next value is the sum of the previous two, so consume_tail checks whether the remaining string begins with that number and recurses on the suffix.
Invariant: current is a valid Fibonacci prefix, and s is the unconsumed suffix that must encode the next terms.
Edge cases: The bound is MAX=2**31, but the usual constraint is at most 2**31-1, so the code may accept a value one above the allowed maximum. Empty or too-short results are not explicitly checked for length three before returning.
Complexity: Candidate prefix enumeration is O(n²), with recursive string slicing and repeated parsing adding substantial overhead; worst-case time can be exponential in string length.

Task and constraints: Split a digit string into a valid Fibonacci-like sequence of at least three integers within 32-bit signed range.
Idea: Enumerate the first two numbers, then greedily match each required sum against the remaining digit string.
Technique and why it applies: startswith accumulates decimal digits until it equals the target sum or exceeds it. The sequence advances only when the exact sum is found.
Invariant: fib is a valid prefix, and k points to the next unconsumed character.
Edge cases: Leading zeros terminate candidate loops after the single digit zero. MAX_INT is 2**31-1, and the overflow guard checks the sum before addition.
Complexity: The first-two-number loops are O(n²); the greedy tail scan can add O(n) per candidate, giving O(n³) time and O(n) working space.

Task and constraints: Compare two strings after applying backspaces, where # removes the previous character.
Idea: Scan each string backward and yield only characters that survive backspaces.
Technique and why it applies: debt counts pending backspaces. A # increases debt; ordinary characters consume debt before they can be yielded. Comparing the surviving streams checks equality without building edited strings.
Invariant: debt is the number of earlier characters still to skip while scanning backward.
Edge cases: zip_longest is used without importing it, so the snippet fails unless that name is defined externally. The comparison assumes the sentinel fill value cannot be confused with a character yielded by the strings.
Complexity: Each character is scanned once, giving O(n+m) time and O(1) generator state.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two strings are equal after interpreting # as a backspace.
Idea: Generate the surviving characters from each string in reverse and compare the two iterators.
Technique and why it applies: The skip counter consumes characters deleted by later backspaces; zip_longest detects differing lengths as well as differing characters.
Invariant: Each generator yields the final string's characters in reverse order, skipping all erased characters.
Edge cases: Empty strings compare equal. itertools.zip_longest supplies a sentinel for the shorter iterator, which cannot equal a normal character.
Complexity: Both strings are scanned once, so time is O(n+m) and auxiliary space is O(1) aside from iterator state.

Task and constraints: Find the longest contiguous mountain: strictly increasing, then strictly decreasing, with both slopes nonempty.
Idea: Compute increasing-run lengths ending at each index and decreasing-run lengths starting there.
Technique and why it applies: A peak is valid only when both lengths exceed one. Their sum minus one gives the mountain length, counting the peak once.
Invariant: max_up[i] measures the increasing arm ending at i, and max_down[i] measures the decreasing arm beginning at i.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero. The code builds a list from reversed(enumerate(arr)), adding O(n) temporary space.
Complexity: The two passes take O(n) time and the two DP arrays plus reversed list use O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest strict mountain subarray.
Idea: Track the current uphill and downhill lengths in one pass, resetting when a plateau occurs or an ascent follows a descent.
Technique and why it applies: A valid mountain needs both up_len and down_len positive; their sum plus one gives its total length. Resetting prevents adjacent mountains from being combined.
Invariant: up_len and down_len describe the current candidate mountain's increasing and decreasing edge counts.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values reset both counters. A mountain is considered only after a descent has begun, so purely increasing or decreasing arrays return zero.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
